newsitem.title: CHINA: Six indicted in China's Moslem rioting, face death.
newsitem.headline: Six indicted in China's Moslem rioting, face death.

text.p: China has indicted six people in connection with rioting in the restive Xinjiang region in February that left nine dead, and the defendants could face the death sentence if convicted, a court official said on Thursday.
But the official denied allegations by exiled separatists that China would execute two rioters on Thursday, saying no one had been sentenced in the case yet.
"So far we have indicted six people," the official said by telephone from Yining in the Moslem region of Xinjiang.

In February, one of the largest demonstrations for independence in Xinjiang since the 1949 communist takeover turned violent, leaving nine people dead and 198 wounded in Yining, near the region's border with Kazakhstan.
Prosecutors have charged the six with hooliganism and endangering social order, the official said. They could be sentenced to death if convicted of hooliganism.
He declined to name the defendants, saying only that the six were all in their 30s and jobless.
Officials had previously identified the suspected ringleader as Abudu Heilili, 29, of the Uighur ethnic minority.

Heilili had been arrested for leading a less violent anti-Chinese demonstration in Yining in August 1995. He was released following "ideological education", or political indoctrination, officials have said.
On Wednesday, Uighur exiles in Kazakhstan's capital of Almaty said China planned to execute two religious students from the Moslem ethnic group.
The exiles said Abu Khair and Abdu Medchit, both around 25 years old and students in Yining, would probably face a firing squad in the regional capital of Urumqi on Thursday.
On Thursday the exiles backpedalled on when the executions were to take place, saying Beijing intended to execute Uighur students arrested over the riots but did not say when.
About 35 young Uighurs staged a noisy protest outside the Chinese embassy in Kazakhstan, shouting: "East Turkestan!" and "Allahu akbar!" (God is great).
Last month, Urumqi was rocked by a series of bus bombings that killed nine people and wounded 74.

Exiled ethnic Uighurs, who want to create an independent state of "East Turkestan" in Xinjiang, have claimed responsibility for the bombings and vowed to stage more attacks until they gain complete freedom for their homeland.
Chinese diplomats filmed the protesters with video recorders.
The Chinese court official denied there had been any executions.
"We have not sentenced anybody yet," the official said, adding that sentencing was expected in April.

Xinjiang, bordering Afghanistan, Pakistan and three mostly Moslem Central Asian states, was shaken last year by bombings and assassination attempts on officials and Moslem leaders regarded as pro-Beijing.
Authorities intensified a crackdown on separatists and underground religious activity.
Last May, Beijing ordered tighter controls along Xinjiang's lengthy border to block the smuggling of weapons and subversive materials from nearby central Asian states.
